query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a machine learning–guided optimization of severe plastic deformation processes (such as HPHT or HPT) will simultaneously improve phase stability, refine the microstructure, and optimize the mechanical properties of coarse‐grained metallic alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional coarse‐grained metallic alloys (or composites) with separate, less controlled phase distributions and larger grain sizes typical of as-cast or green compact states.
generation.intervention: Apply severe plastic deformation under controlled high-pressure/high-temperature conditions with processing parameters (strain, strain rate, temperature, pressure, time) optimized in real time by a machine learning framework trained on high-dimensional experimental data.
generation.conditions: Processing in a high-pressure apparatus (e.g., HPHT or HPT) at elevated temperatures and/or pressures with high strain, where the machine learning model suggests the optimum parameter set; experiments performed in controlled atmospheres to minimize oxidation and residual porosity.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a hierarchically refined microstructure with coherent phase interfaces (e.g., refined FCC/BCC or dual-phase structures) that mediates improved phase stability and helps balance strength with ductility.
generation.mechanism: Severe deformation induces dynamic recrystallization and microstructure refinement, while optimized processing parameters help control phase boundary evolution and lower residual defects; the machine learning model predicts and fine-tunes these parameters based on prior high-dimensional data, leading to a synergistic improvement across phase stability, grain refinement, and mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional processing, the ML-optimized severe plastic deformation process will produce materials with a reduced grain size, lower porosity, enhanced phase stability, and a simultaneous improvement in strength and ductility as observed by EBSD, TEM characterizations, and mechanical testing.
generation.baseline: Materials processed via traditional severe plastic deformation or thermomechanical treatments with heuristic parameter selection, which generally improve one property at the expense of another (e.g., increased strength but reduced ductility or unstable phase compositions).
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the machine learning–assisted optimization may be limited to alloy systems with similar phase structures and thermomechanical responses, and improvements might be less pronounced in systems lacking sufficient high-quality experimental data or those with exceptionally complex phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative improvements (e.g., exact percentages for grain refinement, strength, or ductility gains) remain uncertain until sufficient data are collected, and the generalizability of the ML predictions to all alloy systems has not been fully validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of coarse-grained metallic alloy samples and split them into two groups. Process one group using conventional HPHT/HPT parameters (determined by heuristics) and the other group using parameters predicted by the machine learning framework. Characterize the final microstructure and mechanical properties using standardized techniques.
measurements: Phase composition and stability via XRD

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples processed with ML-optimized parameters do not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., at least a 20% reduction in average grain size, enhanced phase stability with minimal phase decomposition, and measurable increases in both strength and ductility compared to the conventionally processed samples), then the hypothesis should be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

decision.trend: Early studies addressed phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization in isolation – for example, traditional heat treatments for phase stabilization; mechanical alloying, SPS, and HPT for grain refinement; and separate post‐processing steps for tailored mechanical properties. More recent work (e.g. the HPHT treatment in PMC11087546 and the SPS + HPT route in PMC6926650) has integrated severe deformation under controlled temperature/pressure conditions to induce a hierarchical or refined microstructure with improved phase stability and mechanical performance.
decision.unsolved: Despite these promising integrated routes, identifying the optimal process parameter space (strain, strain rate, temperature profiles) to synergistically and simultaneously refine the microstructure, stabilize the phase, and optimize properties over multiple length scales remains unresolved.
decision.lever: Developing a machine learning framework that leverages high-dimensional experimental data from integrated severe plastic deformation and thermomechanical processing (e.g. HPHT, HPT) to predict and fine-tune key parameters (strain, strain rate, temperature/time profiles) that yield the desired multiscale microstructural and property improvements.
decision.why: The gradual shift from separate, heuristic experiments to integrated processing methods has generated large multiscale datasets. A data‐driven model is a natural next step to systematically navigate and optimize the complex processing landscape, addressing the simultaneous challenges of phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property enhancement.
